$comment: The expected state of every check in the organizers' acceptance report.
run.py always exits 0, so tools/run_acceptance.py gates on the report body.
But gating on 'any FAIL is fatal' cannot work before FEAT-05: five of the
seven checks depend on a gallery, a judge console and a CSV export that do
not exist yet, and a gate that is red from the first commit is a gate
nobody reads. It is the same reason a broken healthcheck is worse than no
healthcheck.
So each check carries an EXPECTATION, and the gate enforces both directions:
- a check marked 'pass' that FAILS  -> the gate is RED. A regression.
- a check marked 'fail' that PASSES -> the gate is RED. This file is
stale, and a stale expectation is worse than none: it teaches a reader
that the report is out of date, which makes them discount the whole
document the next time it is genuinely wrong.
'fail' is a claim about the BUILD, not a target. Nothing here is aspirational;
each entry names the feature that flips it, and the reason field is what a
reviewer reads. Flip an entry only when the feature that owns it is done
AND its acceptance line has passed.
The ratchet is the point: this file must grow monotonically from 'pass' to
fully 'pass', and the only way to move an entry is to build the thing.

gallery is public.reason: FEAT-01. The landing page is public with no auth header. Passing since the first commit.

project from fixtures shown.reason: FEAT-03. The gallery is server-rendered at `/`, its first page is in FIXTURE ORDER and its page size is 24, so all three of Glass Signal, Small Meadow and Deep Compass are on page one. `run.py` slices projects[:3] POSITIONALLY rather than searching, so this is a page-slice property and not a search. The check needs any ONE of them; shipping all three costs nothing and removes the temptation to re-paginate. Asserted in tests/test_gallery.py against titles read out of fixtures.json, not typed.

closed event refuses submissions.reason: FEAT-03, and now for the RIGHT reason, which is the whole point of this entry. The route `/projects/new` exists and accepts POST; the refusal is a literal 403 with no Location header, produced by `assert_open_for_submission` in reviewer/events/deadlines.py, and the response body NAMES that function. `run.py` accepts any 4xx, so a body probe below re-sends the checker's own request and asserts the guard's name comes back — a CSRF rejection, a 401 or a 404 can no longer pass this. That probe is the `submit_refused_by_deadline` precondition, added in FEAT-03 when F-40 stopped being hypothetical.

judge sees own scores.reason: FEAT-05. `GET /api/v1/judge/scores` as judge_a returns 200 with a scope receipt reading `allow-own, 3 of 126`, and every row in it carries judge_a's own `source_key`. The endpoint is a plain Django view rather than a DRF viewset, and that is load-bearing rather than a style choice: DRF populates `request.user` from its own authentication classes and would ignore the one our credential middleware assigns, so every header-only request would arrive anonymous and be refused. Three of the four T2 checks want a 403, so that mistake would have produced three GREEN checks for a reason that has nothing to do with isolation -- F-40, in the most expensive shape available. The `judge_scores_route_exists` precondition below is what makes a 200 here mean something.

judge cannot see peer scores.reason: FEAT-05, and the one that matters most. The route returns judge_a's scores to judge_a, and `?judge=judge_a` sent as judge_b is a LITERAL 403 with an empty body and no Location header, produced by the peer-blind accessor `Review.objects.for_actor_and_subject` -- not a redirect, because run.py follows redirects and a 302 would come back as a 200 and fail this while looking correct in a browser. A 404 is no longer accepted for the wrong reason: the `judge_scores_route_exists` precondition asserts the owner gets a 200, and the `peer_scores_refused_by_scope` probe re-sends the checker's OWN request with its OWN credential and requires the refusal to name the guard that produced it, so a 403 from CSRF or from an unrecognised credential can no longer stand in for the isolation layer.

participant blocked.reason: FEAT-05. `GET /api/v1/judge/scores` as the participant is a 403 with an empty body, no Location, and `X-Refused-By: api.judge_scores.role`. The `participant_scores_refused_by_role` probe asserts the guard, so this is a refusal by the role rule rather than by CSRF -- and the same request on a client with `enforce_csrf_checks=True` is a separate test in `tests/test_api.py`, because a CSRF rejection and a scope rejection are both 403 and only the header tells them apart.

csv export works.reason: FEAT-05. `GET /api/v1/export.csv` as the organizer returns 200 and 126 data rows plus a header. **The header is the fixture's KEY order, `functionality, quality, innovation`** -- neither alphabetical nor the order the values appear in any row (F-04). Getting it backwards transposes two columns in every row of every export and nothing else catches it, because a CSV with the right number of columns in the wrong order is perfectly well formed, so the assertion compares against the order derived from `fixtures.json` and a second test checks every exported value against the database per criterion key, since a correct header with positionally paired values is the same defect with the evidence removed. The export is read through `for_actor(actor)` and refused to a judge with a 403, so it is not a second unscoped path to every score in the portal.

$comment: Conditions that must hold for a 'pass' to mean anything. A 'pass' that
does not meet its precondition is reported as a FALSE PASS and fails the
gate.
This exists because two of the seven checks currently pass for a reason
that has nothing to do with the portal being correct. That is F-11's
lesson applied to ourselves: a check reporting PASS without exercising
the behaviour it names is worse than one reporting FAIL, because it
is believed.
TWO KINDS, and the second is the one FEAT-03 added. A route-existence
rule asks 'is this URL routed at all'. A probe rule sends the checker's
OWN request, with its OWN credential, and asserts on the RESPONSE BODY --
so it can tell a real refusal from a refusal by something else. That
distinction is the entire value of the file: a route that exists and is
refused by CSRF, by a missing login or by an empty .dogfood.toml looks
exactly like a route that exists and is refused by the deadline.

submit_route_exists.why: A 404 is a 4xx, so this check passes while the route is absent. The deadline guard is not being tested at all. Assert the route resolves before believing the PASS.

submit_refused_by_deadline.why: The route existing is not enough. run.py accepts ANY 4xx here, so a CSRF rejection, a 401 for an unrecognised credential, or an emptied [auth] block all report PASS while the deadline is never consulted. This probe repeats the checker's own POST, carrying the [auth] participant header out of the very .dogfood.toml run.py read, and requires the response body to name the guard that refused it. If the credential does not verify, the probe cannot see the marker and the gate goes red — which is the point.

judge_scores_route_exists.why: A 404 is a 401/403, so this check passes while there is nothing to leak. Isolation that is enforced by absence is not isolation. Assert the route returns 200 to the legitimate owner before believing the PASS.

peer_scores_refused_by_scope.why: The route existing is not enough, and neither is a 403. A CSRF rejection, a 401 for an unrecognised credential and a genuine peer refusal are the SAME status code, so a probe that only checked the status would be satisfied by a refusal that never consulted the isolation layer -- which is F-40, filed about this gate. This probe repeats the checker's own GET on the peer URL, carrying the [auth] judge_b header out of the very .dogfood.toml run.py read, and requires the response to NAME the guard that refused it. If the credential does not verify, the probe cannot see the marker and the gate goes red, which is the point. It also requires no Location header, so a 302-to-login -- the D-02 failure mode, and the one that returns 200 to run.py -- is caught here rather than by run.py reporting a mysterious FAIL.

judge_scores_route_exists.why: Same as above: 404 is in the accepted set, so this passes before the route exists.

participant_scores_refused_by_role.why: The same false-pass, one route over. A 404 is a 4xx and satisfies the checker's expectation for a route that does not exist, and a 403 from anything at all satisfies it too. So this probe re-sends the checker's own request with the [auth] participant header and requires the refusal to name the ROLE rule -- not the peer rule, and not CSRF. The two guards being distinguishable is the point: they are different decisions, and a portal that refused participants for the peer reason would pass this check while enforcing the wrong policy.

csv_export_route_exists.why: The organizer row of this one is a 200, so a 404 fails it honestly and this precondition is belt-and-braces rather than a rescue. It is here because the other two T2 routes each needed one for the opposite reason, and a reader should not have to work out which preconditions are load-bearing.

$comment: The gate asserts that every tier named in .dogfood.toml's `claimed` list
appears in the report's `verified` line. That is the rule the organizers
state: claiming T2 and verifying T1 scores as T1, and overclaiming is
the one thing that actually costs points.
`claimed = ["T1"]` as of BREAK-1 on 2026-09-28, where it was decided
against what was green: all three T1 checks pass, and pass for the right
reason (the `submit_refused_by_deadline` probe below). T2 is deliberately
unclaimed - all four of its checks are 'fail' above, because the judge
console, the scoped score endpoint and the CSV export are not built.
TWO tests enforce this, and they are not redundant. `tools/run_acceptance.py`
checks `claimed` against the report's OWN `verified` line, against a
running container; that branch is mutation-tested. The pytest copy
(`test_demo_credentials.py::test_the_claim_names_only_tiers_the_gate_can_verify`)
checks the claim against THIS file's expectations, with no container, so an
overclaim is caught by `just test` before the gate ever runs. It parses the
tier split out of run.py rather than typing it, and mirrors run.py's
prefix lock, so a claim of T2 with a failing T1 check fails for the same
reason run.py would give.
